newsitem.title: JAPAN: WEEK AHEAD - Tokyo stocks braced for diet session.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Tokyo stocks braced for diet session.

text.p: Tokyo stocks are likely to see nervous trading this week, with market participants keeping a close eye on government officials' speeches scheduled for the convening of the Diet, or parliament, on Monday.
"The market will watch the parliamentary session very carefully," said Masaaki Higashida, deputy general manager at Nomura Securities Co Ltd.
On Friday, the market's key barometer -- the Nikkei 225 average -- closed at 18,090.04, up 786.39 points from its closing on January 10.

Market participants are anxious to see if the government will revise the 1997 state budget by postponing a sales tax rise or an end to special income tax cuts, or propose any measures to help support the stock market, brokers said.
The stock market, which had been already on a downward spiral, plunged by more than 2,000 points in the first trading week of this year.
"If nothing surprising comes out of the session, the Nikkei will hover at around 18,000," said Masayuki Matsumoto, an analyst at Dai-Ichi Securities Co Ltd.

Worries that Japan's "Big Bang" five-year financial liberalisation plan, proposed by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto late last year, hit banking, securities and insurers shares which have enjoyed much government protection.
But officials have not so far taken any steps to support the stock market, except to reiterate that they were watching developments carefully and that they would implement reforms steadily.

Earlier this week, Taku Yamazaki, chairman of the policy-making committee of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, was quoted by Jiji news agency as urging the government to consider measures to tackle the problem of weak Tokyo stocks.
Some brokers said that they would wait and see if the ruling party hammered out any effective measures.

They added the market could be overshadowed for the next few months by expectations that Japanese companies might sell part of their shareholdings to take profits ahead of their book closings at the end of March.
"Possible profit-taking is likely to put a lid on the stock market between January and March," Nomura's Higashida said.

Kenjiro Hata, the chairman of the Life Insurance Association of Japan, said on Friday that some life insurers may sell domestic and foreign bonds and stocks if Tokyo stock prices did not recover, Jiji news agency reported.

Nomura's Higashida noted that long positions had still accumulated in the Nikkei 225's futures market, even after the latest sharp deline, and unwinding of these positions could hit the Nikkei 225 lower.
Any slips in the New York stock exchange could also send the Japanese stocks under selling pressure, he added.
